title: African American Genealogy & Freedmen's Bureau Records

subChunks.title: Crossing the 1870 Wall — Research Strategies for African American Ancestors
subChunks.hookHtml: For millions of Americans, the genealogical trail hits a wall at 1870 — the first census in which formerly enslaved people appear by name as free citizens. Before that year, enslaved ancestors were enumerated only as numbers in the slave schedules; their names, families, and origins were systematically suppressed by the institution of slavery. African American genealogy is among the most challenging and the most important work in the field: challenging because slavery deliberately obscured identity; important because recovering these identities is an act of historical justice. A set of specialised records — above all, the Freedmen's Bureau records — provides the keys to crossing the 1870 wall.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The 1870 wall — what it means and why it exists

The 1870 census was the first US federal census to record all individuals by name regardless of race. Before emancipation (1865), enslaved people appeared in two ways:

  • Slave schedules (1850 and 1860 censuses): a separate schedule listing slave-holders by name and their enslaved people by age and sex only — no names. An entry might read: 'Thomas Jefferson: enslaved persons — 1 male age 40, 1 female age 35, 1 male age 15...' The individuals are completely unnamed.
  • Free Black population: free persons of colour were enumerated by name in the regular census schedules from 1790 onward. Before 1870, a named African American in the census was almost certainly free-born or manumitted.

The 1870 wall strategy is: establish the full family in 1870 (names, ages, birthplaces), then work backwards using Freedmen's Bureau records, plantation records, slaveholder research, and the 1865–1870 bridge records to cross into the slavery era.

Freedmen's Bureau records — the most important source

The Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands (the Freedmen's Bureau) operated from 1865 to 1872. It was established to manage the transition from slavery to freedom, and it generated an extraordinary quantity of records documenting the lives of formerly enslaved people:

  • Labour contracts: contracts between freedpeople and former enslavers or new employers, often giving full name, age, former enslaver's name, and county of origin. These are the most genealogically dense record type.
  • Marriage registers: the Bureau recorded the marriages of formerly enslaved people — often the first legal record of a marriage that had existed for years or decades. These registers give both spouses' names, ages, former enslaver's names, and sometimes the names of children.
  • Ration and claims records: lists of freedpeople receiving food, medical care, or transportation assistance — giving names and ages.
  • Letters and complaints: freedpeople wrote to or filed complaints with Bureau agents about labour disputes, violence, family separation, and searches for missing relatives. These letters are sometimes the most personal and detailed records: a woman searching for children sold away from her; a man looking for a wife taken to another state.
  • Hospital and death records: freedmen's hospitals kept admission and mortality records, giving names and sometimes place of origin.

Freedmen's Bureau records are now largely digitised through a partnership between FamilySearch, the Smithsonian, and Howard University. They are searchable free at FamilySearch.org and Freedmensbureau.com.

The slaveholder research strategy

A key method for crossing the 1870 wall is researching the slaveholder family. After 1870, formerly enslaved people often:

  • Adopted the surname of their former enslaver (the most common pattern, though not universal)
  • Remained in the same county or on the same land as sharecroppers or tenant farmers
  • Named children after members of the slaveholder family

The research approach: identify the likely slaveholder from the 1870 census (look for white families of the same surname living nearby, or use tax records and estate records); find that family in the 1850 and 1860 slave schedules; match ages and sex of enslaved people in the schedules against your ancestor's family ages in 1870. This is not proof — it is a hypothesis requiring corroboration — but it establishes the framework for further research.

Additional record sources

  • Southern Claims Commission (1871–1880): Union loyalists in the South (including many freedpeople) could claim compensation for property taken by the Union army. Approved and rejected claims contain detailed testimony about the claimant's life before and during the war, including sometimes pre-war family history. Accessible via Fold3 and FamilySearch.
  • Church records: African American churches — African Methodist Episcopal (AME), Baptist, and later Pentecostal — maintained separate registers from the antebellum period. Many historically Black church records are at state archives, the Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture (New York), and Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs) in the relevant states.
  • Freedmen's Savings Bank records: the Freedman's Savings and Trust Company (1865–1874) kept detailed signature card registers listing depositors' names, ages, birthplaces, physical descriptions, occupations, and family members. The cards are searchable free at FamilySearch.
  • Plantation records and estate papers: some plantation owners kept detailed records of enslaved people — birth registers, death records, medical records, even baptismal entries. These are held at state archives, university special collections (particularly Southern universities), and sometimes still in private family collections. The Born in Slavery collection (Library of Congress) digitised many narratives; Race & Slavery Petitions Project at UNC-Greensboro indexes petitions involving enslaved people.
  • 1865 Slave Narrative interviews (WPA): the Works Progress Administration conducted oral history interviews with formerly enslaved people in the 1930s. These interviews — held at the Library of Congress and digitised online — sometimes name specific enslavers, plantations, and family members. Not genealogically reliable on their own but valuable for context and leads.

DNA and African American genealogy

DNA testing plays a particularly important role in African American research precisely because documentary records were systematically suppressed. Autosomal DNA can identify cousins who share an enslaved ancestor even when no paper trail survives. African ancestry reference populations on platforms like 23andMe and AncestryDNA can help identify broad regional origins in Africa. The African American DNA Roots Project at FamilyTreeDNA focuses on Y-DNA and mtDNA deep ancestry. DNA is not a substitute for documentary research but is a powerful complement, particularly for locating living cousins whose family lines preserved oral histories or records that have since been lost.

storyBeats.text: Theodora places a wide, flat ledger on the table — the 1860 slave schedule for Sumter District, South Carolina. The columns show ages and sexes only. No names. Row after row of nameless human beings.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: This is what the archive looks like before 1865 for enslaved ancestors. Not invisibility — erasure. Deliberate, systematic, legal erasure. The slave schedule records that a man aged forty-two existed, that a woman aged thirty-eight existed, that a boy aged fourteen existed. It does not tell you their names. It does not tell you that they were a family. It tells you only what the law required: that they were property, enumerated as numbers.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: The Freedmen's Bureau records change this. From 1865 to 1872, Bureau agents across the South recorded labour contracts, marriages, rations, letters, complaints. The labour contract gives you: William Anderson, aged 42, formerly enslaved by James Heyward of Sumter District, contracted to work on the Heyward plantation for the 1866 season. His wife, Mary, aged 38. Their son, Thomas, aged 14. Three names — real names — in a document created the year after emancipation. That is your bridge across 1870.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: And the Freedman's Savings Bank — do not overlook it. The signature card register for each depositor asks: name, age, birthplace, occupation, physical description, and family members. A freedman depositing his first wages was asked to describe his family. Many did. The cards are on FamilySearch, free, and they are sometimes the most detailed record of an individual's family that was ever created.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Anchor African American genealogy strategies

Retrieve from memory:

  • What is the '1870 wall' and why does it exist?
  • Name three record types generated by the Freedmen's Bureau and the genealogical information each provides.
  • What is the slaveholder research strategy and what are its limitations?
  • What are the Freedman's Savings Bank records and what information do they contain?
  • How does DNA testing complement documentary research in African American genealogy?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
The '1870 wall' is the genealogical barrier created by the institution of slavery: the 1870 census was the first in which all Americans were enumerated by name. Before emancipation, enslaved people appeared only as unnamed numbers (age and sex) in the slave schedules of 1850 and 1860, making it nearly impossible to trace individuals through documentary records before 1865.

Three Freedmen's Bureau record types: (1) Labour contracts — give full name, age, former enslaver's name, and county of origin; (2) Marriage registers — record legal marriages of formerly enslaved people with both spouses' names, ages, former enslaver, and sometimes children's names; (3) Letters and complaints — personal testimony about family separation and searches for missing relatives, sometimes the most detailed personal record that exists.

The slaveholder research strategy involves identifying the likely slaveholder from the 1870 census (often a white family of the same surname living nearby), then locating that family in the 1850 and 1860 slave schedules to match ages and sex of enslaved people against the ancestor's family. Limitation: this is a hypothesis requiring corroboration from other sources (Bureau records, estate papers), not proof in itself — surname adoption was common but not universal.

Freedman's Savings Bank records are signature cards for depositors of the Freedman's Savings and Trust Company (1865–1874), giving name, age, birthplace, physical description, occupation, and family members. They are free on FamilySearch.

DNA testing identifies cousins who share an enslaved ancestor even when documentary records do not survive; African ancestry reference populations give broad regional origins; DNA connects living cousins who may have preserved oral histories or other records.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Crossing the 1870 wall — designing a research strategy

You are researching Eliza Johnson (b. c.1840, Georgia), who appears in the 1870 census in Hancock County, Georgia, as head of household, age 30, with children: Samuel (12), Harriet (10), and James (6). Her race is listed as Black. You believe she was enslaved before 1865.

Design a research strategy (300–400 words) explaining step-by-step how you would attempt to establish Eliza's identity before 1865, the records you would consult, and how you would evaluate evidence.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Step 1 — Establish the post-1865 record base: Search Freedmen's Bureau records for Hancock County, Georgia, for Eliza Johnson or any woman named Eliza whose ages match (c.1840). Labour contracts, marriage registers, and ration records for this county are on FamilySearch. If a labour contract names Eliza Johnson with children matching the 1870 ages, this establishes her post-war family unit and likely names her former enslaver.

Step 2 — Freedman's Savings Bank: Search the signature card index on FamilySearch for Eliza Johnson or her husband (if a marriage register turns up a husband who died before 1870). Hancock County residents may have accounts at the Augusta, Georgia branch.

Step 3 — Slaveholder research: 'Johnson' as a surname strongly suggests former enslavement by a Johnson family. In the 1870 Hancock County census, identify white Johnson families living nearby. Cross-reference with the 1860 slave schedule: search for Johnson slaveholders in Hancock County whose slave schedules show a woman aged approximately 20 in 1860 (matching Eliza's birth c.1840) and children matching Samuel (b.c.1858) and Harriet (b.c.1860). The 1860 schedule gives only ages and sex — match by age range.

Step 4 — Estate and plantation records: If a specific Johnson slaveholder is identified, search for their probate records, estate inventories, and will (Georgia state archives, Hancock County probate records). Estate inventories sometimes listed enslaved people by name. A will might bequeath 'my woman Eliza and her children' to a named heir.

Step 5 — DNA testing: Eliza's living descendants should test at AncestryDNA. A shared match network in Hancock County with both white Johnson descendants and African American families who share the Johnson surname may corroborate the slaveholder identification.

Evaluation: No single source proves the connection. The research succeeds if multiple independent sources converge: a Bureau record naming Eliza, a slave schedule age match, and an estate record mentioning an Eliza. Each corroborates the others. If sources conflict, document the conflict and continue searching.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Separate census schedules from 1850 and 1860 listing enslaved people by age and sex only (no names) under the name of the slaveholder — the primary source for establishing the existence of an enslaved individual before 1865.

The Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands (1865–1872), whose records — labour contracts, marriage registers, letters, and ration lists — are the most important source for crossing the 1870 wall in African American research.

Signature card registers for depositors of the Freedman's Savings and Trust Company (1865–1874), giving name, age, birthplace, physical description, and family members — available free on FamilySearch.
A body (1871–1880) that adjudicated claims for property taken by the Union army; claimants' testimony (including from freedpeople) can provide detailed pre-war family history not found elsewhere.

Oral history interviews conducted in the 1930s by the Works Progress Administration with formerly enslaved people, held at the Library of Congress — valuable for context and research leads, but not genealogically reliable without corroboration.

questions.questionHtml: What is the '1870 wall' in African American genealogy?
options: The 1870 census was the first to enumerate all Americans by name; before this, enslaved people appeared only as unnamed numbers in slave schedules, making it difficult to trace individuals before 1865
The US government destroyed all records created before 1870 relating to slavery
African American families were not permitted to own property before 1870 and therefore left no records
The 1870 census recorded only white Americans by name; Black Americans were first enumerated in 1880
questions.correctAnswer: The 1870 census was the first to enumerate all Americans by name; before this, enslaved people appeared only as unnamed numbers in slave schedules, making it difficult to trace individuals before 1865
questions.explanationHtml: The 1870 census was the first US federal census taken after emancipation in which all Americans — regardless of race — were enumerated by name. Before emancipation, enslaved people appeared only in the 1850 and 1860 slave schedules as unnamed individuals listed by age and sex under the slaveholder's name. The wall is not a legal barrier created after 1870 but the consequence of systematic erasure under slavery. The 1865–1870 Freedmen's Bureau records, Freedman's Savings Bank records, and other bridge sources provide strategies for crossing this barrier.

questions.questionHtml: You are researching an African American ancestor, Daniel Freeman, who appears in the 1870 census in Edgefield County, South Carolina, aged 45. You cannot find him before 1865. Which is the most productive next step?
options: Search Freedmen's Bureau records for Edgefield County, South Carolina, on FamilySearch — labour contracts, marriage registers, and ration lists may name Daniel Freeman and identify his former enslaver
Search US passenger lists for a Daniel Freeman arriving from Africa before 1865
Assume Daniel Freeman changed his name after emancipation and search the 1860 regular census for a white Daniel Freeman of the same age
Wait until the 1900 census to find him at age 75 and work forward
questions.correctAnswer: Search Freedmen's Bureau records for Edgefield County, South Carolina, on FamilySearch — labour contracts, marriage registers, and ration lists may name Daniel Freeman and identify his former enslaver
questions.explanationHtml: The Freedmen's Bureau records are the primary bridge source for the period 1865–1872. Labour contracts for Edgefield County were recorded by Bureau agents and often give the freedperson's full name, age, former enslaver's name, and location. If Daniel Freeman signed a labour contract in 1866 or 1867, it should appear in the digitised Bureau records on FamilySearch (free). The marriage register is also worth checking if Daniel may have had a spouse — it gives both partners' former enslaver details. These records directly address the 1870 wall by creating a name-bearing document in the immediate post-emancipation period.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher uses the slaveholder research strategy: they identify the Smith family as the likely former enslaver of their ancestor Celia Smith (b. c.1845), based on shared surname and proximity in 1870. They find a woman aged approximately 25 in the Smith family's 1860 slave schedule. They conclude this proves Celia was enslaved by the Smiths. Is this conclusion correct?
options: No — the slave schedule shows only ages and sexes, not names; the surname adoption pattern is common but not universal; the age match establishes a plausible hypothesis that must be corroborated by Freedmen's Bureau records, estate papers, or other primary sources before it becomes a conclusion
Yes — the surname match plus the age match in the slave schedule is definitive proof of identity
No — enslaved people never took the surname of their former enslaver, so a surname match disproves the connection
Yes — the 1860 slave schedule entry is a primary source and therefore constitutes proof
questions.correctAnswer: No — the slave schedule shows only ages and sexes, not names; the surname adoption pattern is common but not universal; the age match establishes a plausible hypothesis that must be corroborated by Freedmen's Bureau records, estate papers, or other primary sources before it becomes a conclusion
questions.explanationHtml: The slaveholder research strategy is a hypothesis-generation tool, not a proof mechanism. Its limitations are significant: (1) the slave schedule names no one — only the slaveholder is named; the enslaved people are listed by age and sex only; (2) surname adoption after emancipation was common but not universal — some freedpeople chose different surnames to signal a break from their enslaver; (3) an age match of 'approximately 25 in 1860' against Celia's birth year of c.1845 leaves room for error in age reporting (both in the schedule and in the 1870 census). The hypothesis requires corroboration: a Freedmen's Bureau labour contract for Celia Smith naming the Smith family as former enslavers, a Smith estate inventory naming Celia, or a marriage register entry identifying her former enslaver as Smith. Without corroboration from a separate source, the age match in the slave schedule is a lead, not a proof.
